messages.author: e808374824de43c9
messages.subject: Spatial Data with Replicates
parts:
Hey everyone,
As the title suggests, I have binary spatial data with multiple people living in the same ZIP code. I want to model the spatial covariance using a gaussian process (essentially a logistic regression with spatially correlated random effects). Right now, the way this looks in the code is something like the following.

data{
  y // outcome vector
  zip // recoded zip code vector (1, 2, ..., # of zip codes)
}

parameters{
...
mu;
eta_squared;
s_squared;
jitter_z;
W_z;
}

transformed parameters{
...
s <- pow(s_squared, 0.5);
eta <- pow(eta_squared,0.5);

Sigma_decomp <- cholesky_decompose(eta_squared*exp(-rho*D)); // D is the distance matrix, eta_squared and rho are parameters
W <- Sigma_decomp*W; // Spatial random effects
jitter <- s*jitter
}

model{
  W_z ~ normal(0,1);
  jitter_z ~ normal(0,1);

  W_new <- W*eta;
  b <- W_new[zip] + jitter;

  y ~ bernoulli_logit(mu + b);
}

I'm wondering whether there is a more efficient way to code this up, maybe by moving b into the transformed parameters block for example and getting rid of W_new by multiplying eta to W directly in the transformed parameters block. My dataset has a few thousand records, and including the jitter makes it take a long time to run, so any help would be much appreciated. 

Also, the first time I ran this code, I forgot to put a prior on jitter_z, but things still ran (albeit with terrible mixing). As kind of an under the hood thing, is Stan just putting vague priors on parameters that aren't given explicit priors?

Hey Mike,
I think that in my current implementation of the Stan code I'm using that cholesky factor implementation for all of the spatial random effects. It looks like the main differences are that (trying to use your notation here)

1) I don't define covMat before L, instead going for "L <- cholesky_decompose(exp(-rho*dx))" where dx is the distance matrix. Not sure if that makes a big difference, but I was trying to avoid the looping
2) Since I have multivariate data (two sets of random effects), I take f and make it an nX x 2 matrix (call it f_new).
3) For each outcome vector y[i], instead of saying y[i] ~ Normal(f_new[XY,1],noise), I am saying y[i] <- f_new[XY,i] + jitter[i], where jitter[i] ~ N(0,noise[i]). My thinking was that if I move the RVs into the parameters block it might speed things up, but i'm not sure that's actually the case.

The other thing I should point out is that since it's two binary outcomes, I don't think the model is identifiable unless I fix noise[1] and eta[1], but that's not really applicable to your code. Thanks for all your input and feedback, and let me know if there's something I am misunderstanding.
